{{Short description|Theorem in optics that explains light propagation in a medium}}
In [[optics]], the '''Ewald–Oseen extinction theorem''', sometimes referred to as just the '''extinction theorem''', is a theorem that underlies the common understanding of scattering (as well as refraction, reflection, and diffraction). It is named after [[Paul Peter Ewald]] and [[Carl Wilhelm Oseen]], who proved the theorem in crystalline and isotropic media, respectively, in 1916 and 1915.<ref name=born_and_wolf>{{Citation| author=Born, Max| author2=Wolf, Emil|title=[[Principles of Optics]]|edition=7th|publisher=Cambridge University Press|place=Cambridge| year=1999|page=[https://books.google.com/books?id=oV80AAAAIAAJ&pg=PA106 106]| isbn=9780521784498| author2-link=Emil Wolf| author-link=Max Born}}</ref> Originally, the theorem applied to scattering by isotropic [[dielectric]] objects in free space. The scope of the theorem was greatly extended to encompass a wide variety of bianisotropic media.<ref name=lakhtakia>{{Citation|last=Lakhtakia|first=Akhlesh| year=2017|title=The Ewald-Oseen Extinction Theorem and the Extended Boundary Condition Method, in: The World of Applied Electromagnetics| publisher=Springer|place=Cham, Switzerland| pages=481–513| doi=10.1007/978-3-319-58403-4_19| chapter=The Ewald–Oseen Extinction Theorem and the Extended Boundary Condition Method| isbn=978-3-319-58402-7}}</ref>

== Overview ==

An important part of optical [[physics]] theory is starting with microscopic physics—the behavior of atoms and electrons—and using it to ''derive'' the familiar, macroscopic, laws of optics. In particular, there is a derivation of how the [[refractive index]] works and where it comes from, starting from microscopic physics. The Ewald–Oseen extinction theorem is one part of that derivation (as is the [[Lorentz–Lorenz equation]] etc.).

When light traveling in vacuum enters a transparent medium like glass, the light slows down, as described by the [[index of refraction]]. Although this fact is famous and familiar, it is actually quite strange and surprising when you think about it microscopically. After all, according to the [[superposition principle]], the light in the glass is a superposition of:
* The original light wave, and
* The light waves emitted by oscillating electrons in the glass.

(Light is an oscillating [[electromagnetic field]] that pushes electrons back and forth, emitting [[dipole radiation]].)

Individually, each of these waves travels at the [[speed of light]] in vacuum, ''not'' at the (slower) speed of light in glass. Yet when the waves are added up, they surprisingly create ''only'' a wave that travels at the slower speed.

The Ewald–Oseen extinction theorem says that the light emitted by the atoms has a component traveling at the speed of light in vacuum, which exactly cancels out ("extinguishes") the original light wave. Additionally, the light emitted by the atoms has a component which looks like a wave traveling at the slower speed of light in glass. Altogether, the ''only'' wave in the glass is the slow wave, consistent with what we expect from basic optics.

A more complete description can be found in Classical Optics and its Applications, by Masud Mansuripur.<ref name=mansuripur>{{Citation|last=Mansuripur|first=Masud|year=2009|title=Classical Optics and its Applications (2nd ed.)|publisher=Cambridge University Press|place=Cambridge| page=209|chapter-url=https://books.google.com/books?id=Nrkfmf4RizIC&pg=PA168| doi=10.1017/CBO9780511803796.019| arxiv=1507.05234|chapter=The Ewald–Oseen extinction theorem|isbn=9780511803796}}</ref>  A  proof of the classical theorem can be found in ''[[Principles of Optics]]'', by Born and Wolf,<ref name=born_and_wolf/> and that of its extension has been presented by [[Akhlesh Lakhtakia]].<ref name=lakhtakia/>

== Derivation from Maxwell's equations ==

=== Introduction ===
When an electromagnetic wave enters a dielectric medium, it excites (resonates) the material's electrons whether they are free or bound, setting them into a vibratory state with the same frequency as the wave. These electrons will in turn radiate their own electromagnetic fields as a result of their oscillation (EM fields of oscillating charges). Due to the linearity of Maxwell equations, one expects the total field at any point in space to be the sum of the original field and the field produced by oscillating electrons. This result is, however, counterintuitive to the practical wave one observes in the dielectric moving at a speed of c/n, where n is the medium index of refraction. The Ewald–Oseen extinction theorem seek to address the disconnect by demonstrating how the superposition of these two waves reproduces the familiar result of a wave that moves at a speed of c/n.

=== Derivation ===
The following is a derivation based on a work by Ballenegger and Weber.<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Ballenegger|first=Vincent C.| last2=Weber|first2=T. A.|date=1999-07-01| title=The Ewald–Oseen extinction theorem and extinction lengths| url=https://aapt.scitation.org/doi/10.1119/1.19330| journal=American Journal of Physics | volume=67|issue=7|pages=599–605 |doi=10.1119/1.19330|issn=0002-9505|url-access=subscription}}</ref> Let's consider a simplified situation in which a monochromatic electromagnetic wave is normally incident on a medium filling half the space in the region z>0 as shown in Figure 1.
[[File:Dielectric_half_space.svg|thumb|Figure 1: The half-space z>0 is a dielectric material with susceptibility χ. The half-space z<0 is vacuum.]]
The [[electric field]] at a point in space is the sum of the electric fields due to all the various sources. In our case, we separate the fields in two categories based on their generating sources. We denote the incident field
<math display="block"> \mathbf{E}_{\mathrm{vac}} </math>
and the sum of the fields generated by the oscillating electrons in the medium
<math display="block"> \mathbf{E}_{\mathrm{rad}}(z, t).</math>

The total field at any point z in space is then given by the superposition of the two contributions,
<math display="block">\mathbf{E}(z, t)= \mathbf{E}_{\mathrm{vac}}(z, t) + \mathbf{E}_{\mathrm{rad}}(z, t).</math>

To match what we already observe, <math>\mathbf{E}_{\mathrm{vac}}</math> has this form. However, we already know that inside the medium, z>0, we will only observe what we call the transmitted E-field <math>\mathbf{E}_{\mathrm{T}}</math> which travels through the material at speed c/n.

Therefore, in this formalism,
<math display="block">\mathbf{E}_{\mathrm{rad}}(z, t) = -\mathbf{E}_{\mathrm{vac}}(z, t) + \mathbf{E}_{T}(z, t)</math>

This to say that the radiated field cancels out the incident field and creates a transmitted field traveling within the medium at speed c/n. Using the same logic, outside the medium the radiated field produces the effect of a reflected field <math>\mathbf{E}_{R}</math> traveling at speed c in the opposite direction to the incident field.
<math display="block">\mathbf{E}_{\mathrm{rad}}(z, t) = -\mathbf{E}_{\mathrm{vac}}(z, t) -\mathbf{E}_{R}(z, t)</math>
assume that the wavelength is much larger than the average separation of atoms so that the medium can be considered continuous. We use the usual macroscopic E and B fields and take the medium to be nonmagnetic and neutral so that [[Maxwell's equations]] read
<math display="block">\begin{align}
\nabla \cdot \mathbf{E}&=0 \\
\nabla \cdot \mathbf{B}&=0 \\
\nabla \times \mathbf{E}&=-\frac {\partial \mathbf{B}} {\partial t} \\
\nabla \times \mathbf{B}&=\boldsymbol{\mu}_{0} \mathbf{J}+\epsilon_{0} \boldsymbol{\mu}_{0} \frac{\partial \mathbf{E}}{\partial t}
\end{align}</math>
both the total electric and magnetic fields
<math display="block">\mathbf{E}=\mathbf{E}_{\mathrm{vac}}+\mathbf{E}_{\mathrm{rad}}, \quad \mathbf{B}=\mathbf{B}_{\mathrm{vac}}+\mathbf{B}_{\mathrm{rad}}</math>
the set of Maxwell equations inside the dielectric
<math display="block">\begin{array}{l}
{\nabla \cdot \mathbf{E}_{\mathrm{rad}}=0} \\
{\nabla \cdot \mathbf{B}_{\mathrm{rad}}=0} \\ {\nabla \times \mathbf{E}_{\mathrm{rad}}=-\partial \mathbf{B}_{\mathrm{rad}} / \partial t} \\ {\nabla \times \mathbf{B}_{\mathrm{rad}}=\mu_{0} \mathbf{J}+\epsilon_{0} \mu_{0} \partial \mathbf{E}_{\mathrm{rad}} / \partial t}
\end{array}</math>
where <math>\mathbf{J}</math> includes the true and polarization current induced in the material by the outside electric field. We assume a linear relationship between the current and the electric field, hence
<math display="block">\mathbf{J}={\sigma} \left(\mathbf{E}_{\mathrm{vac}} + \mathbf{E}_{\mathrm{rad}}\right)</math>

The set of Maxwell equations outside the dielectric has no [[current density]] term
<math display="block">\begin{array}{l}
{\nabla \cdot \mathbf{E}_{\mathrm{vac}}=0} \\
{\nabla \cdot \mathbf{B}_{\mathrm{vac}}=0} \\
{\nabla \times \mathbf{E}_{\mathrm{vac}}=-\partial \mathbf{B}_{\mathrm{vac}} / \partial t} \\
{\nabla \times \mathbf{B}_{\mathrm{vac}}=\epsilon_{0} \mu_{0} \partial \mathbf{E}_{\mathrm{vac}} / \partial t}
\end{array}</math>

The two sets of Maxwell equations are coupled since the vacuum electric field appears in the current density term.

For a monochromatic wave at normal incidence, the vacuum electric field has the form
<math display="block">\mathbf{E}_{\mathrm{vac}}(z, t)=\mathbf{E}_{\mathrm{vac}} \exp [i(k z- \omega t)],</math>
with <math>k=\omega /{c}</math>.

Now to solve for <math>\mathbf{E}_{\mathrm{rad}}</math>, we take the curl of the third equation in the first set of Maxwell equation and combine it with the fourth.
<math display="block">\begin{align}
\nabla\times(\nabla\times \mathbf{E}_{\mathrm{rad}}) &= -\frac \partial {\partial t} (\nabla\times\mathbf{B}_{\mathrm{rad}}) \\[1ex]
\nabla\times(\nabla \times \mathbf{E}_{\mathrm{rad}}) &= - \frac \partial {\partial t} \left(\mu_{0} \mathbf{J}+\epsilon_{0} \mu_{0} \frac{\partial \mathbf{E}_{\mathrm{rad}}} {\partial t}\right)
\end{align}</math>

We simplify the double curl in a couple of steps using [[Einstein notation#Common operations in this notation|Einstein summation]].
<math display="block">\begin{align}
\nabla\times(\nabla \times \mathbf{E})_{i}
&=
\epsilon_{i j k}\epsilon_{k l m} \partial_{j} \partial_{l} E_{m}
\\&=(\delta_{i l} \delta_{j \mathrm{m}}-\delta_{i \mathrm{m}} \delta_{j l})\partial_{j} \partial_{l} E_{m}
\\&=\partial_{i}(\partial_{j}E_{j})-\partial_{j}\partial_{j} E_{i}
\end{align}</math>

Hence we obtain,
<math display="block">\nabla\times(\nabla \times \mathbf{E}_{rad})=\nabla(\nabla\cdot\mathbf{E}_{rad})-\nabla^2\mathbf{E}_{rad}</math>

Then substituting <math>\mathbf{J}</math> by <math>{\sigma} \left(\mathbf{E}_{\mathrm{vac}} + \mathbf{E}_{\mathrm{rad}}\right)
</math>, using the fact that <math>\nabla\cdot\mathbf{E}_{\mathrm{rad}} = 0</math> we obtain,
<math display="block">\nabla^2\mathbf{E}_\mathrm{rad} = \frac \partial {\partial t}(\mu_{0}{\sigma}\mathbf{E}_{\mathrm{vac}} + \mu_0 {\sigma} \mathbf{E}_{\mathrm{rad}} + \epsilon_{0} \mu_{0} \partial \mathbf{E}_{\mathrm{rad}} / \partial t)</math>

Realizing that all the fields have the same time dependence <math>\exp (-i \omega t)
</math>, the time derivatives are straightforward and we obtain the following inhomogeneous wave equation
<math display="block">\nabla^{2} \mathbf{E}_{\mathrm{rad}}+\mu_{0} \omega^{2}\left(\epsilon_{0}+i \sigma / \omega\right) \mathbf{E}_{\mathrm{rad}}= -i \mu_{0} \omega \sigma \mathbf{E}_{\mathrm{vac}}(z)</math>
with particular solution
<math display="block">\mathbf{E}_{\mathrm{rad}}^{P} = -\mathbf{E}_{\mathrm{vac}}(z)</math>

For the complete solution, we add to the particular solution the general solution of the homogeneous equation which is a superposition of plane waves traveling in arbitrary directions
<math display="block"> \left(\mathbf{E}_{\mathrm{rad}}^{c}\right)_{i} = \int g_{i}(\boldsymbol{\theta}, \boldsymbol{\phi}) \exp \left(i \mathbf{k}' \cdot \mathbf{r}\right) d \Omega</math>
where <math>k' </math> is found from the homogeneous equation to be
<math display="block">k^{\prime 2}=\mu_{0} \epsilon_{0} \omega^2 \left(1+i \frac{\sigma}{\epsilon_{0} \omega}\right)</math>

Note that we have taken the solution as a coherent superposition of plane waves. Because of symmetry, we expect the fields to be the same in a plane perpendicular to the <math>z</math> axis. Hence <math>\mathbf{k}' \cdot \mathbf{a} = 0,</math> where <math>\mathbf a</math> is a displacement perpendicular to <math>z</math>.

Since there are no boundaries in the region <math>z>0</math>, we expect a wave traveling to the right. The solution to the homogeneous equation becomes,
<math display="block">\mathbf{E}_{\mathrm{rad}}^{c} = \mathbf{E}_{T} \exp \left(i k' z\right)</math>

Adding this to the particular solution, we get the radiated wave inside the medium (<math>z > 0</math>)
<math display="block">\mathbf{E}_{\mathrm{rad}} = -\mathbf{E}_{\mathrm{vac}}(z) + \mathbf{E}_{T} \exp \left(i k' z\right)</math>

The total field at any position <math>z</math> is the sum of the incident and radiated fields at that position. Adding the two components inside the medium, we get the total field
<math display="block">\mathrm{E}(z) = \mathrm{E}_{T} \exp \left(i k' z\right), \qquad z>0</math>

This wave travels inside the dielectric at speed <math>c/n,</math>
<math display="block">n = c k' / \omega = \sqrt{1+i \frac{\sigma}{\epsilon_{0} \omega}}</math>

We can simplify the above  <math>n</math> to a familiar form of the index of refraction of a linear isotropic dielectric. To do so, we remember that in a linear dielectric an applied electric field <math>\mathbf E</math> induces a polarization <math>\mathbf P</math> proportional to the electric field <math>\mathbf P = \epsilon_{0} \chi_{e} \mathbf{E}</math>. When the electric field changes, the induced charges move and produces a current density given by <math>\partial \mathbf{P} / \partial t</math>. Since the time dependence of the electric field is <math>\exp(-i\omega t)</math>, we get
<math display="block">\mathbf{J}=-i \epsilon_{0} \omega \chi_{e} \mathbf{E},</math>
which implies that the conductivity
<math display="block">\sigma=-i \epsilon_{0} \omega \chi_{e}.</math>

Then substituting the conductivity in the equation of <math>n</math>, gives
<math display="block">n=\sqrt{1+\chi_{e}}</math>
which is a more familiar form. For the region <math>z<0</math>, one imposes the condition of a wave traveling to the left. By setting the conductivity in this region   <math>\sigma=0</math>, we obtain the reflected wave
<math display="block">\mathrm{E}(z) = \mathrm{E}_{R} \exp \left(-i k z\right),</math>
traveling at the speed of light.

Note that the coefficients nomenclature, <math>\mathbf E_{T} </math> and <math>\mathbf E_{R}</math>, are only adopted to match what we already expect.

== Hertz vector approach ==
The following is a derivation based on a work by Wangsness <ref>{{Cite journal| last=Wangsness|first=Roald K.| date=1981-10-01| title=Effect of matter on the phase velocity of an electromagnetic wave|journal=American Journal of Physics| volume=49|issue=10|pages=950–953| doi=10.1119/1.12596|issn=0002-9505| bibcode=1981AmJPh..49..950W}}</ref> and a similar derivation found in chapter 20 of Zangwill's text, Modern Electrodynamics.<ref>{{Cite book|title=Modern Electrodynamics|last=Zangwill|first=Andrew|publisher=Cambridge University Press| year=2013| isbn=9780521896979}}</ref> The setup is as follows, let the infinite half-space <math>z<0</math> be vacuum and the infinite half-space <math>z>0</math> be a uniform, isotropic, dielectric material with [[electric susceptibility]], <math>\chi.</math>

The [[inhomogeneous electromagnetic wave equation]] for the electric field can be written in terms of the electric [[Hertz vector|Hertz Potential]], <math> 
\boldsymbol{\pi}_{\mathrm{e}}
</math>, in the [[Lorenz gauge condition|Lorenz gauge]] as
<math display="block"> 
\nabla^{2} \boldsymbol{\pi}_{\mathrm{e}}-\frac{1}{c^2} \frac{\partial^{2} \boldsymbol{\pi}_{\mathrm{e}}}{\partial t^{2}}=-\frac{\mathbf{P} }{\epsilon_{0}}.
</math>

The electric field in terms of the Hertz vectors is given as
<math display="block">\mathbf{E}=\nabla \times \nabla \times \boldsymbol\pi_{\mathrm{e}}-\frac{\mathbf{P}}{\epsilon_{0}}-
\frac{\partial}{\partial t}
\left(\nabla \times \boldsymbol{\pi}_{\mathrm{m}}
\right),</math>
but the magnetic Hertz vector <math> 
\boldsymbol{\pi}_{\mathrm{m}} </math> is 0 since the material is assumed to be non-magnetizable and there is no external magnetic field. Therefore, the electric field simplifies to
<math display="block">\mathbf{E} = \nabla \times \nabla \times \boldsymbol\pi_{\mathrm{e}} - \frac{\mathbf{P}}{\epsilon_{0}}.</math>

In order to calculate the electric field we must first solve the inhomogeneous wave equation for <math> \boldsymbol{\pi}_{\mathrm{e}} </math>. To do this, split <math> \boldsymbol{\pi}_{\mathrm{e}} </math> in the homogeneous and particular solutions
<math display="block">
\boldsymbol{\pi}_{\mathrm{e}}(\mathbf{r}, t) = \boldsymbol{\pi}_{e,h}(\mathbf{r}, t) + \boldsymbol{\pi}_{\mathrm{e,p}}(\mathbf{r}, t).</math>

Linearity then allows us to write
<math display="block">
\mathbf{E}(\mathbf{r}, t)=\mathbf{E}_{h}(\mathbf{r}, t)+\mathbf{E}_{\mathrm{p}}(\mathbf{r}, t).
</math>

The [[Homogeneous differential equation|homogeneous solution]], <math>
\mathbf{E}_{h}(\mathbf{r}, t)
</math>, is the initial [[plane wave]] traveling with wave vector <math> k_0 = \omega/c </math> in the positive <math>z</math> direction
<math display="block"> \mathbf{E}_{h}(\mathbf{r}, t) = \mathbf{E}_{0} e^{i\left(k_{0} z - \omega t\right)} . </math>

We do not need to explicitly find <math>
\boldsymbol{\pi}_{e,h}(\mathbf{r}, t)
</math> since we are only interested in finding the field.

The particular solution, <math>
\boldsymbol{\pi}_{\mathrm{e,p}}(\mathbf{r}, t)</math> and therefore, <math>
\mathbf{E}_{\mathrm{p}}(\mathbf{r}, t)
</math>, is found using a time dependent [[Green's function]] method on the inhomogeneous wave equation for <math> 
\boldsymbol{\pi}_{\mathrm{e,p}}
</math> which produces the [[Retarded potential|retarded]] integral
<math display="block"> \boldsymbol{\pi}_{\mathrm{e,p}}(\mathbf{r}, t) = \frac{1}{4 \pi \epsilon_{0}} \int d^3 r' \frac{\mathbf{P}\left(\mathbf{r}', t - \left|\mathbf{r}-\mathbf{r}'\right| / c\right)}{\left|\mathbf{r}-\mathbf{r}'\right|}. </math>

Since the initial electric field is polarizing the material, the polarization vector must have the same space and time dependence <math>\mathbf{P}(\mathbf{r}, t) = \mathbf{P}_{0} e^{i(k z-\omega t)}.</math> More detail about this assumption is discussed by Wangsness. Plugging this into the integral and expressing in terms of Cartesian coordinates produces
<math display="block">
\boldsymbol{\pi}_{\mathrm{e,p}}(\mathbf{r}, t)= \frac{\mathbf{P}_{0} e^{ i(k z-\omega t)}} {4 \pi \epsilon_{0}} \int_{0}^{\infty} dz' e^{ i k\left(z'-z\right)} \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} dx' \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} dy' \frac{e^{ i k_0 \left|\mathbf{r}-\mathbf{r}'\right|}}{\left|\mathbf{r}-\mathbf{r}'\right|}.
</math>

First, consider only the integration over <math>x' </math> and <math>y'</math> and convert this to [[Cylindrical coordinate system|cylindrical coordinates]] <math>(x,y,z)\rightarrow(\rho,\varphi,z) 
</math> and call <math> \left|\mathbf{r}-\mathbf{r}'\right| = R</math>
<math display="block">
I:=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} d x^{\prime} \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} d y^{\prime} \frac{e^{ i k_{0}\left|\mathbf{r}-\mathbf{r}^{\prime}\right|}}{\left|\mathbf{r}-\mathbf{r}^{\prime}\right|}
=
\int_{0}^{2\pi} d \varphi' \int_{0}^{\infty} d \rho' \frac{e^{ i k_0 R}}{R}
=
2\pi \int_{0}^{\infty} d \rho' \frac{e^{ i k_{0}R}}{R}.
</math>

Then using the substitution
<math display="block">R^{2}=\rho^{2}+\left|z'-z\right|^{2} 
\Rightarrow 
\rho^{2} = R^{2}-\left|z'-z\right|^{2} 
\Rightarrow 
\rho \, d \rho = R \,  dR
</math>
and
<math display="block">\rho=\sqrt{R^2-\left|z'-z\right|^2} 
</math>
so the limits become
<math display="block">\rho=0=\sqrt{R^{2}-\left|z'-z\right|^{2}} \Rightarrow R=\left|z'-z\right|
</math>
and
<math display="block">\rho = \infty=\sqrt{R^2-\left|z'-z\right|^2} \Rightarrow R=\infty.
</math>

Then introduce a convergence factor <math>e^{-\epsilon R} </math> with <math>\epsilon \in \R</math> into the integrand since it does not change the value of the integral,

<math display="block">
\begin{align}
I &=
2\pi \int_{\left|z'-z\right|}^{\infty} d R e^{ i k_{0}R}
\\&=
2\pi \lim_{\epsilon \to 0}\int_{\left|z'-z\right|}^{\infty} d R e^{(i k_{0}-\epsilon)R}
\\&=
\left. 2\pi \lim_{\epsilon \to 0} \left[\frac{e^{(i k_{0}-\epsilon)R}}{i k_{0}-\epsilon}\right]
\right|_{\left|z'-z\right|}^\infty
\\&=
 2\pi \lim_{\epsilon \to 0} \left[\frac{e^{(i k_{0}-\epsilon)\infty}}{i k_{0}-\epsilon}-\frac{e^{(i k_{0}-\epsilon){\left|z'-z\right|}}}{i k_{0}-\epsilon}\right].
\end{align} 
</math>

Then <math>\epsilon \in \R</math> implies <math>\lim_{\epsilon \to 0}  e^{-\epsilon\infty}=0 </math>, hence <math>\lim_{\epsilon \to 0} e^{(i k_{0}-\epsilon)\infty} = \lim_{\epsilon \to 0}e^{i k_{0}\infty} e^{-\epsilon\infty}=0
</math>. Therefore,
<math display="block">
\begin{align}
I &=
 2\pi \lim_{\epsilon \to 0} \left[0-\frac{e^{(i k_{0}-\epsilon){\left|z^{\prime}-z\right|}}}{i k_{0}-\epsilon}\right]
\\&=
 -2\pi \frac{e^{i k_{0}{\left|z'-z\right|}}}{i k_{0}}
\\&=
 2\pi i \frac{e^{i k_{0}{\left|z'-z\right|}}}{k_{0}}.

\end{align} 
</math>

Now, plugging this result back into the z-integral yields
<math display="block">
\boldsymbol{\pi}_{\mathrm{e,p}}(z, t)= \frac{i\mathbf{P}_{0}

e^{ i(k z-\omega t)}

}{2 k_{0}\epsilon_{0}} \int_{0}^{\infty} d z'

e^{ i k\left(z'-z\right) }

e^{ i k_{0}\left|z-z'\right|}
</math>

Notice that <math>
\boldsymbol{\pi}_{\mathrm{e,p}}
</math> is now only a function of <math>
z</math> and not <math>\mathbf{r}</math>, which was expected for the given symmetry.

This integration must be split into two due to the absolute value <math>\left|z-z' \right|</math> inside the integrand. The regions are <math>z<0</math> and <math>z>0</math>. Again, a convergence factor must be introduced to evaluate both integrals and the result is
<math display="block"> \boldsymbol{\pi}_{\mathrm{e,p}}(z, t)=-\frac{\mathbf{P}e^{ -i \omega t}} {2 \epsilon_{0} k_{0}}

\begin{cases}
{{\frac{1}{k+k_{0}} e^{ -i k_{0} z}}} & {z<0} 
\\ {\frac{2 k_{0}}{k_{0}^{2}-k^{2}} e^{ i k z}
+
\frac{1}{k-k_{0}} e^{ i k_{0} z}} & {z>0.}
\end{cases}</math>

Instead of plugging <math>
\boldsymbol{\pi}_{\mathrm{e,p}}
</math> directly into the expression for the electric field, several simplifications can be made. Begin with the [[Vector calculus identities#Curl of the curl|curl of the curl vector identity]],
<math display="block">
\nabla \times(\nabla \times \mathbf{\boldsymbol{\pi}_{\mathrm{e,p}}})=\nabla(\nabla \cdot \mathbf{\boldsymbol{\pi}_{\mathrm{e,p}}})-\nabla^{2} \mathbf{\boldsymbol{\pi}_{\mathrm{e,p}}},
</math>
therefore,
<math display="block">
\begin{align}
\mathbf{E}_{\mathrm{p}}
&=
\nabla \times \nabla \times \boldsymbol\pi_{\mathrm{e}}-\frac{\mathbf{P}}{\epsilon_{0}}
\\&=
\nabla(\nabla \cdot \boldsymbol{\pi}_{\mathrm{e,p}})-\nabla^{2} \boldsymbol{\pi}_{\mathrm{e,p}}-\frac{\mathbf{P}}{\epsilon_{0}}.
\end{align}
</math>

Notice that <math>\nabla \cdot \boldsymbol{\pi}_{\mathrm{e,p}} = 0</math> because <math>\mathbf{P}</math> has no <math>{\mathbf{z}}</math> dependence and is always perpendicular to <math>\hat{\mathbf{z}}</math>. Also, notice that the second and third terms are equivalent to the inhomogeneous wave equation, therefore,
<math display="block"> \begin{align}
\mathbf{E}_{\mathrm{p}}
&=
-\frac{1}{c^{2}} \frac{\partial^{2} \boldsymbol{\pi}_{\mathrm{e,p}}}{\partial t^{2}} 
\\&=
-\frac{1}{c^{2}} (-i\omega)^2 \boldsymbol{\pi}_{\mathrm{e,p}}
\\&=
k_{0}^2 \boldsymbol{\pi}_{\mathrm{e,p}}
\end{align}
</math>

Therefore, the total field is
<math display="block">
\mathbf{E}(z, t)=\mathbf{E}_{0} 
e^{i\left(k_{0} z-\omega t\right)}
+k_{0}^{2} \boldsymbol\pi_{\mathrm{e,p}}(z, t)
</math>
which becomes,
<math display="block">\mathbf{E}(z, t)
=
\left\{\begin{array}{l}
{\mathbf{E}_{0} e^{i\left(k_{0} z-\omega t\right)}-\frac{\mathbf{P}}{2 \epsilon_{0}} \frac{k_{0}}{k+k_{0}} e^{-i\left(k_{0} z+\omega t\right)}} & {z<0} \\ 
{\mathbf{E}_{0} e^{i\left(k_{0} z-\omega t\right)}-\frac{\mathbf{P}}{2 \epsilon_{0}} \frac{k_{0}}{k-k_{0}} e^{i\left(k_{0} z-\omega t\right)}-\frac{\mathbf{P}}{\epsilon_{0}} \frac{k_{0}^{2}}{k_{0}^{2}-k^{2}} e^{i(k z-\omega t)}} & {z>0.}
\end{array}\right.</math>

Now focus on the field inside the dielectric. Using the fact that <math>
\mathbf{E}(z, t) </math> is complex, we may immediately write
<math display="block">
\mathbf{E}(z>0, t) = \mathbf{E} 
e^{i\left(k_{0} z-\omega t\right)}
</math>
recall also that inside the dielectric we have <math>\mathbf{P} =\epsilon_{0} \chi \mathbf{E}</math>.

Then by coefficient matching we find,
<math display="block">
e^{i\left(k z-\omega t\right)}
\Rightarrow
1=-\chi \frac{k_{0}^{2}}{k_{0}^{2}-k^{2}}
</math>
and
<math display="block">
e^{i\left(k_{0} z-\omega t\right)}
\Rightarrow

0=\mathbf{E}_{0}-\frac{\chi}{2} \frac{k_{0}}{k-k_{0}} \mathbf{E}.
</math>

The first relation quickly yields the [[wave vector]] in the dielectric in terms of the incident wave as
<math display="block">
\begin{align}
k
&=\sqrt{1+\chi} k_{0}

\\&=n k_{0}.
\end{align}
</math>

Using this result and the definition of <math>
\mathbf{P} </math> in the second expression yields the polarization vector in terms of the incident electric field as
<math display="block">
\mathbf{P}
=
2 \epsilon_{0}(n-1) \mathbf{E}_{0}.
</math>

Both of these results can be substituted into the expression for the electric field to obtain the final expression
<math display="block">\mathbf{E}(z, t)
=
\left\{\begin{array}{l}
{\mathbf{E}_{0} e^{i\left(k_{0} z-\omega t\right)}

-\left(\frac{n-1}{n+1}\right) \mathbf{E}_{0} e^{-i\left(k_{0} z+\omega t\right)}} & {z<0} \\ 
{\left(\frac{2}{n+1}\right) \mathbf{E}_{0} e^{i\left(n k_{0} z-\omega t\right)}} & {z>0.}
\end{array}\right.</math>

This is exactly the result as expected. There is only one wave inside the medium and it has wave speed reduced by n. The expected reflection and transmission coefficients are also recovered.

== Extinction lengths and tests of special relativity ==

The characteristic "extinction length" of a medium is the distance after which the original wave can be said to have been completely replaced. For visible light, traveling in air at [[sea level]], this distance is approximately 1&nbsp;mm.<ref name=fox62>{{Citation|author=Fox, J.G. |title=Experimental Evidence for the Second Postulate of Special Relativity |journal=American Journal of Physics | volume=30|issue=1|year=1962|pages=297–300 |doi=10.1119/1.1941992 |bibcode=1962AmJPh..30..297F |postscript=. |author-link=J. G. Fox}}</ref> In interstellar space, the extinction length for light is 2 light years.<ref name=brecher>{{Cite journal |author=Brecher, K.|title=Is the speed of light independent of the velocity of the source|journal=Physical Review Letters |volume=39|year=1977|pages=1051–1054 |doi=10.1103/PhysRevLett.39.1051 |bibcode=1977PhRvL..39.1051B|issue=17}}</ref>  At very high frequencies, the electrons in the medium can't "follow" the original wave into oscillation, which lets that wave travel much further:  for 0.5 MeV gamma rays, the length is 19&nbsp;cm of air and 0.3&nbsp;mm of Lucite, and for 4.4 GeV, 1.7 m in air, and 1.4&nbsp;mm in carbon.<ref name=filippas_and_fox>{{cite journal| last=Filippas|first=T.A.|author2=Fox, J.G.| title=Velocity of Gamma Rays from a Moving Source|journal=Physical Review| year=1964| volume=135|issue=4B| pages=B1071–1075| bibcode = 1964PhRv..135.1071F |doi = 10.1103/PhysRev.135.B1071 |author2-link=J. G. Fox}}</ref>

[[Special relativity]] predicts that the speed of light in vacuum is independent of the velocity of the source emitting it. This widely believed prediction has been occasionally tested using astronomical observations.<ref name=fox62/><ref name=brecher/> For example, in a [[binary star]] system, the two stars are moving in opposite directions, and one might test the prediction by analyzing their light.  (See, for instance, the [[De Sitter double star experiment]].)  Unfortunately, the extinction length of light in space nullifies the results of any such experiments using visible light, especially when taking account of the thick cloud of stationary gas surrounding such stars.<ref name=fox62 />  However, experiments using X-rays emitted by binary pulsars, with much longer extinction length, have been successful.<ref name=brecher /> Other controversial experiments have also been conducted at the [[Navy Electronics Laboratory]] to test the speed of light emitted from moving sources.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Kantor |first=Wallace |date=1962-09-01 |title=Direct First-Order Experiment on the Propagation of Light from a Moving Source |url=https://opg.optica.org/abstract.cfm?URI=josa-52-9-978 |journal=Journal of the Optical Society of America |language=en |volume=52 |issue=9 |pages=978 |doi=10.1364/JOSA.52.000978 |issn=0030-3941|url-access=subscription }}</ref>
